source: Uganda MoH Essential Maternal Guidelines / WHO Emergency Obstetric Care

entries.text: POSTPARTUM HEMORRHAGE (PPH) — LEADING CAUSE OF MATERNAL DEATH: PPH is heavy bleeding after delivery (soaking more than 2 pads in 30 minutes). This is an EMERGENCY. IMMEDIATE ACTIONS at community level: (1) Call for help and arrange URGENT transport to health facility. (2) Rub the uterus firmly in a circular motion through the abdomen (uterine massage). The uterus should feel firm like a ball. (3) Encourage the mother to breastfeed immediately (helps the uterus contract). (4) If available, give Misoprostol 800mcg under the tongue (ONLY if trained). (5) Keep the mother warm. (6) Elevate her legs. (7) Give fluids by mouth if she is conscious. (8) Do NOT pack the vagina with cloth. (9) REFER IMMEDIATELY — PPH kills within 2 hours without treatment. Every minute counts.

ECLAMPSIA (CONVULSIONS IN PREGNANCY): Eclampsia is convulsions (fits) in a pregnant woman or within 48 hours after delivery, usually caused by very high blood pressure. This is a LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY. SIGNS: Severe headache, blurred vision, upper abdominal pain, swelling of face and hands, then sudden convulsions. IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: (1) Protect the woman from injury — move hard objects away, place her on her side. (2) Do NOT put anything in her mouth. (3) Do NOT restrain her during the fit. (4) After the fit: keep her on her side (recovery position). (5) Check breathing — if not breathing, tilt head back and lift chin. (6) REFER IMMEDIATELY to the nearest health facility. (7) If available and trained: give Magnesium Sulfate injection. (8) Keep environment quiet and dark. Eclampsia can recur — the woman needs emergency care.

CHOKING — FIRST AID: FOR ADULTS AND CHILDREN OVER 1 YEAR: (1) Encourage coughing — if the person can cough, let them try to clear it. (2) If they cannot breathe, speak, or cough: Stand behind them, lean them slightly forward. (3) Give 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. (4) If still choking: Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) — stand behind, place fist above navel, pull sharply inward and upward. Repeat up to 5 times. (5) Alternate: 5 back blows, 5 abdominal thrusts. (6) If person becomes unconscious: lay them flat, call for help, begin CPR if trained. FOR INFANTS UNDER 1 YEAR: (1) Lay baby face down along your forearm, supporting the head. (2) Give 5 back blows between shoulder blades. (3) Turn baby face up. Give 5 chest thrusts (2 fingers on breastbone). (4) Look in mouth — remove visible object. (5) Repeat. NEVER do blind finger sweeps in a baby's mouth.

SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION (ANAPHYLAXIS): Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that can happen within minutes. Common causes: insect stings (bees, wasps), certain foods (groundnuts, fish), medications. SIGNS: Difficulty breathing, swelling of lips/tongue/throat, widespread rash/hives, dizziness or fainting, fast heartbeat, feeling of doom. WHAT TO DO: (1) Call for emergency help immediately. (2) If the person has an adrenaline injector (EpiPen): help them use it in the outer thigh. (3) Lay the person flat with legs elevated (unless they have breathing difficulty — let them sit up). (4) If not breathing: begin CPR if trained. (5) REFER TO HEALTH FACILITY IMMEDIATELY. (6) Do NOT give anything by mouth. (7) Monitor breathing continuously. Anaphylaxis can be fatal within minutes without treatment.

CORD PROLAPSE — OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord comes out through the cervix ahead of or alongside the baby after the membranes have ruptured. This is a LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY for the baby because the cord gets compressed, cutting off the baby's blood and oxygen supply. RECOGNITION: (1) You can see or feel the cord at the vagina after the waters break. (2) The cord may be pulsating. (3) Sudden severe fetal heart rate changes (if monitoring available). IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: (1) Call for help and arrange URGENT transport to a facility with surgical capacity (CEmONC — Caesarean section needed). (2) KNEE-CHEST POSITION: Help the mother get on her knees with her chest down and buttocks elevated — this uses gravity to take pressure off the cord. Alternatively: Trendelenburg position (lie flat with legs elevated higher than head). (3) If the cord is visible, gently push it back and hold it with a warm, wet, clean cloth — do NOT compress it. (4) Do NOT try to push the cord back in forcefully. (5) Keep the cord moist with warm saline or clean warm water on a cloth. (6) REFER IMMEDIATELY — the baby needs emergency delivery (usually Caesarean section) within minutes. (7) Do NOT let the mother push or bear down. (8) Give nothing by mouth (prepare for possible surgery). Every minute counts — delay leads to brain damage or death of the baby.

entries.text: RETAINED PLACENTA — OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: The placenta should deliver within 30 minutes after the baby is born. If it has not delivered after 30-60 minutes, it is retained. This is dangerous because it can cause severe bleeding (postpartum haemorrhage) and infection. SIGNS: (1) Placenta not delivered within 30-60 minutes of delivery. (2) The cord may appear to be lengthening but placenta does not come out. (3) Bleeding may be heavy or may be hidden (trapped behind the placenta). (4) The uterus may feel soft (not contracted). IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: (1) DO NOT PULL ON THE CORD — this can cause the uterus to turn inside out (uterine inversion), which is life-threatening. (2) Encourage the mother to breastfeed immediately — this stimulates uterine contractions. (3) Encourage the mother to empty her bladder (a full bladder can prevent placental delivery). (4) If trained: controlled cord traction with counter-pressure on the uterus (Brandt-Andrews technique) — ONLY if trained. (5) Give Oxytocin 10 IU IM if not already given (only if trained and available). (6) Monitor for signs of shock: fast pulse, low blood pressure, pale, sweaty, confused. (7) REFER IMMEDIATELY to a facility that can perform manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia. (8) Start IV fluids during transport if trained. Do NOT attempt manual removal at community level — this requires anaesthesia and sterile conditions.

entries.text: SHOULDER DYSTOCIA — OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: Shoulder dystocia occurs when the baby's head has delivered but the shoulders are stuck behind the mother's pubic bone. This is an EMERGENCY — the baby can die within minutes from compression of the cord and lack of oxygen. RECOGNITION: (1) The baby's head delivers but then retracts tightly against the perineum ('turtle sign'). (2) The head has delivered but no further progress despite maternal pushing. (3) The baby's face may become congested (blue/purple). IMMEDIATE ACTIONS — CALL FOR HELP: (1) Tell the mother to STOP PUSHING. (2) McROBERTS MANOEUVRE (first-line): Lay mother flat on her back. Two helpers each take one of her legs and push her knees sharply up toward her chest (hyperflexing the hips). This flattens the pelvis and usually frees the shoulder. (3) Apply SUPRAPUBIC PRESSURE: An assistant pushes downward and laterally just above the pubic bone (NOT on the top of the uterus — fundal pressure can worsen the impaction). (4) If the baby delivers — immediate newborn care and resuscitation if needed. (5) Do NOT pull on the baby's head — this can cause nerve damage (brachial plexus injury). (6) Do NOT apply fundal pressure (pushing on top of the uterus). (7) REFER IMMEDIATELY if McRoberts and suprapubic pressure do not work — the mother needs emergency intervention at a CEmONC facility. (8) After delivery, check for PPH and perineal tears. Document the event for the facility team.
